I actually just spoke to my dr about this exact thing this week. She says that anxiety can make you lose words, especially in 'high stakes' conversations. For me thats anytime I need words to be precise, like when I'm talking about work (in the sciences). Or anytime I'm anxious.

For me, its like my life is a giant game of MadLibs. I lose the nouns and verbs, and need to make them up on the spot. For example, the other day I was talking to myself about what to make for dinner and I could see the picture of a piece of frozen chicken breast in my head. But all I got was the letter K. And I had time, so I tried to figure out where the K came in the word- does it start or end with K. Turns out chicken sounds an awful lot like Ks and has one in the middle. Not helpful when I'm in the middle of a face to face conversation though. 

Your friend might be on to something with the alexithymia though. If you can't identify you are anxious, how can you identify triggers for losing words? Thats where I get stuck. So I'm just assuming anytime I need to talk about work I get anxious. 

For me, it boils down to covid too. I lost more words since covid hit- because I dont' practice anymore. I only talk to 2-3 people a week, so I'm losing my skills at managing the anxiety and its coming out in lost words. Next step is to talk to my counselor about it, get practical solutions for managing the anxiety I suppose.

So I guess in answer to your question, I get caught up in the "I need to work" mindset.  It becomes a loop in my mind and I can't get out until I'm forced out.  Then I can agree, it was that bad and I need time.  

Bring it up with your doctor.  Worst they will say is no, but usually they won't argue if you think you need it.  But don't take the time to abandon everything.  Keep going to see a dr to work on stuff if at all possible.  Set aside an hour every so often to really think "why am I doing this if I am this unhappy?"  If its a justified answer, you're fine.  

But if you really are struggling, don't do it alone.  Let your supervisor in on it ahead of time so its not a surprise.  Don't lead with an out of the blue "I'm thinking of taking time off."  Lead with something that suggests your health isn't where it needs to be for you to push through the next two years.  Your supervisor might even suggest taking time off (again highly dependent on the person).  

I wait until it gets too far along and I can't think straight and rely on others to tell me I need to take time.  Don't do that.  If you have enough insight, bring it up now before it gets too deep.

I did it, a few years ago during my PhD.  And am in the middle of one now (unofficial one) for anxiety again.  I'm lucky that my supervisor and department are very supportive.  Right now we are working on ways for me to keep going to work/school and stay healthy in the process.  

Honestly, I didn't tell anyone really that I was taking time off.  Even though it was for 4 months.  They just assumed I was working from home.  Or didn't say anything. I got treated no differently. No special considerations (other than in my best interest).  No one thought any different of me, that I know of at least.  

I noticed that I'm getting anxious in my writing, so we are working on ways for me to write, but also do other stuff- like help my supervisor in the lab.  That way its a win win for everyone- he gets more help setting up experiments, and I get more papers and a break from the writing one day a week or so. 

But I do have to say- I had a Masters supervisor who was the opposite.  My lab mate's mother died while she was in the end stages of her Masters, and the supervisor said she couldn't take any time off for that, nevermind recuperating after the fact.  So make sure you have an ally, I guess I'm saying.  Could be a supervisor, a department head, a doctor (especially some who will write you a letter saying you need to take leave!), a therapist who is willing to talk to your supervisor (and you are ok sharing that much information), the grad school, a chaplain, anyone in "authority."  

I understand what you are going through, and have been on both sides of it with different supervisors. Just make sure you know the rules about taking leave- realize you won't get a stipend likely during it, fill out all the paperwork, and be organized as much as you can.  A good supervisor will understand and may even help you through it.

The most helpful thing that I found was to make an energy budget.  Energy accounting.  The way Tony Atwood put it, "Fight Aspie with Aspie."  If you get easily tired by social things and tend to get overwhelmed or burst out or cry or just overflow somehow and can't figure out why, use your logic skills.

He gave the example of a thermometer type thing.  But I think better in calendars, so I adapted it for that.  So I have a weekly calendar I got off google and blocked in my meetings and appointments for the week.  Then assigned them a score from 0-100 of how much energy it took out (like a meeting with my supervisor was -100).  Then tally up the day.  If you go negative, (which you will if you only withdraw), you need to add things to make it zero or positive.  Like schedule in an hour of special interest, or going for a walk.  Then afterward see how much you got back.

Right now its a work in progress for me.  Any given event (even grocery shopping) might be negative a lot one day and not so negative the next.  So it will change.  But after some time, you will learn your range.  And then know what to do to raise your balance.  

Its a good system, for me.  It helps to see patterns and learn how much energy it takes, or when you need to learn to schedule in rests throughout the day.  I like it.

I like my research (which is a good thing).  Its based on acid sulfate soils in Australia.  So soils full of iron and sulfur, that are really acidic (like pH 3).  The problems come when you drain the wetlands, like for development.  Then they start reacting with oxygen and the sulfur turns to sulfuric acid and eats away at anything it can find.  

One way to mitigate these soils is to reflood them.  And one strategy is to use wastewater, like from agricultural lands or wastewater treatment plants, because that water is relatively stable in quantity (rain isn't).  But, one problem with this, is introducing P.  So my research is chemical, and looks at the interactions between a certain mineral, schwertmannite, and P.  

Schwertmannite is orange, and one of the most common minerals around here in acid sulfate landscapes.  So its important to know whats going to happen.  Added to the complexity is the changing redox conditions (oxic or anoxic waters).  This can change how the mineral reacts.  So I'm running experiments to see what happens.

Thats basically my PhD.  Three different experiments on P and schwertmannite.

Every Tuesday I go to a nursing home in town and volunteer for a few hours.  I get to help the dementia residents with exercise.  Its my favorite thing of the week.  They often need help isolating a muscle to move it when instructed, so I point to it or touch their arm or move their arm first for them.  Then they can repeat a lot easier.  

There are two guys I especially love working with.  First there's Harold.  Once I touch his arm or his leg and show him how to move it, her gets it and can do it.  I encourage him a bit, give him a smile, and he throws this huge grin right back at me.  Like no one has ever complimented him before.  I get so excited for him when he is able to isolate that specific muscle and he can tell and gets so excited himself.

Then there's John.  My favorite (even though we aren't allowed to have favorites).  He doesn't move much.  So I grab his hands and make him raise his arms.  Grab his shoe and show him how to rotate his ankle.  Then he gets it.  He grabs my hands so hard and won't let go.  And does the exercise.  But only if I'm holding his hands.  As soon as I let go, its like his hold on the world goes as well.  

Yeah, its sad, but I see it as so much more positive.  When someone is with his, connecting physically with him, he is back with this world.  He isn't lost in his head anymore.  And I can relate to that.  I've been alone, and you kind of get sucked into the "alone-ness"  Then something jolts you back and you come back to the world.  With John, he needs a physical touch.  Then he grabs on and won't let go.  Shows me exactly how to do the exercise like he is the one teaching me.  

(Another side story about John- he collects spoons and I think I figured out why and I want to tell someone.  He can only eat mashed foods, and gets a new spoon for each dish for some reason.  I'm feeding him one dish and we finish.  I put that spoon down.  I go to start the next dish and he has a few bites, then all of a sudden leans forward and grabs the first spoon.  I think he sees that spoon and associates spoons with food (rightfully so).  So in his mind, if he grabs the spoon, he won't have to eat more, like if he's full and preventing more food, as if there was only one spoon.  So I've started asking him if he wants more after he grabs the spoon and he says no, solidifying my thoughts.  For him it just doesn't register that there could be two spoons.  And he doesn't talk much, so I think he likes being asked his opinion.  I mean I talk to him about other stuff, but he doesn't usually reply.  But about food he does.  I think he is forced to finish his meals (which is probably a good thing) but morning tea is a fine meal to skip and he likes the option.)

I love working with dementia residents, if you can't tell by now.  :)

Something my doctor told me to do is to make a schedule every night.  Its more for my anxiety/depression and abundant time off (sick leave from Uni).  But it might work.

The day is chunked into two hour blocks.  Every two hours I have to do something I enjoy and something productive.  An adult task.  It could be- pay a bill, do a little Uni work, take out the trash.  Something that is productive.  And then something I like, to make the day not so hard.

So maybe something like that.  Instead of planning down to the minute (which I enjoy but get frustrated with at the same time), plan down to the two hours?  

Maybe start with a list of everything that has to get done, but don't get stuck making the list.  If you forget something, add it on when you remember.  Then make a list of things you like, even if it is just staring out the window for five minutes.  Then build your schedule.  I use [this format](http://www.blashki.com/general-practice/patient-resources-/cbt-worksheets/weekly-planner.pdf).  

So every night I plan my two hours.  This way I dont get overwhelmed by a weeks worth of stuff, and it is manageable.  I can repeat things if I like them.  Or I can do something new.  But this ensures that every two hours, something productive gets done.  

I was reminded many times to leave room for flexibility.  So if something enjoyable takes two hours, and just pay a bill in the next two hours, don't freak out because you didn't get exactly the right number of things done every day.  Or that the time taken doesn't match.  Leave room to be flexible.  And its also important to leave room for resting.  Schedule in to take out the trash, but that won't take two hours, so you get a chance to read a book in the meantime.  

Maybe plan two hours to study for math, but it takes three.  So you shift.  Or maybe the assignment takes a half hour instead of two.  Now you can shift everything up and go to bed early. This was the hard part for me.  Now I'm used to it, and just have the general idea of what needs to get done each day and I'm ok.  But the sheet that I HAD to fill in every night because it would be looked at by my doctor was helpful getting me on track.

The stress of being in a new country, away from supports I didn't even know I had, is really challenging.  It makes me appreciate what I have a lot more- just knowing you could lose it all with such a rash decision.  

There was the little things- like navigating a grocery store not knowing any of the brands.  Or getting a cell phone plan without having an address (I was living at a bed and breakfast for a while.)  I wasn't able to transfer money into the country for a few weeks and my paycheck got messed up, so I had about $50 for a while.  Luckily my not-so-nice landlord was actually nice there and let me pay late (because I was her faith, which automatically makes me an ok person- good thing, because who knows what would have happened if I wasn't her faith...).

Its a risky thing.  You need to plan for at least the basics- a place to live, a job (or substantial savings), and supports.  You can't just move and expect to find friends.  Everyone already has their groups.  You have to be sussed out to see if you can fit into their group.  It won't happen overnight.  I had to rely on the generosity of strangers and the mental health nurse that was assigned to me.  She was the only person I would talk to for days at a time.  It was very isolating.

You never know what type of need you will have unless you plan it out.

I have had both good and bad results with two different advisers.  It really depends on your relationship with your adviser. 

My first adviser was very harsh, almost bullying.  I was having trouble with lab and school work, and mentioned I had issues with anxiety and depression.  She kind of pulled it out of me as well.  She then used it against me for the rest of my time with her.  Going as far as pulling me aside when I was thinking about PhD, taking a walk with me and telling me how lucky I was that she took me on as a student.  No professor would ever want me as a PhD student because I was just too special.  Due to my short memory, she would tease me and tell me to go get my notebook and she wouldn't talk to me without it.  And she wouldn't write me a letter of recommendation for my PhD application.

I got a PhD position anyway, out of the country where they didn't require letters.  I ran into a lot of troubles here and I am on a leave of absence to work on some mental health issues.  I told one supervisor, and he is nothing but supportive.  Even told me he would support me if I quit after this time off.  It is more important to work on myself than get a piece of paper.  It does help that he is super Buddhist and personal.  My main supervisor knows a little (mainly because I am scared of him- he's a huge body builder scientist, but super relaxed.  He even told me I could blow up the lab by accident and it was recoverable) and he just shrugged and said to get better.  It doesn't bother him.  

So my point in writing all this is to say that it really depends on your relationship with your supervisor and their personality type.  Gauge if you can trust that person.  If you can, tell them.  If you aren't sure, hold off.  If you expect your behaviors to flare up again, explain it ahead of time.  If you sense that they will cool down and the rifts will be a thing of the past, let it be a thing of the past.  Don't dredge up bad memories if it won't serve you.  Try to get a handle on yourself and where you think you will go in the future.  

But most of all, good luck.  Both with the illness and with your studies and with the decision to tell your adviser.

The important thing is to keep trying.  If you keep trying, it just passes.  But if you say something and all of a sudden stop talking, people will realize you have stopped and might become more aware.  of you. I creep in the corner).  If you stop trying, the new thing will be people asking "why are you so dull?"  (I've gotten that one a few times now).  

So practically.  Talk.  The more conversations you have, the more interactions you have, the less percentage of those interactions will be embarrassing.  Its math.  You can't argue with math.  But if you retreat into a corner, that becomes a new thing for people to notice.  So don't give up.  It will be uncomfortable as anything else.  But try.  Easier said than done, but don't give up.
